analysis.one_liner: Bans fuel price gouging during emergencies and directs the fines to help poor families pay energy bills.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote in the 110th Congress, dying in House subcommittee after referral in May 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it a federal offense for companies selling crude oil, gasoline, or heating fuels to raise prices by an "unconscionable" amount during an emergency the President declares — such as a hurricane or war that disrupts fuel supply. The Federal Trade Commission could impose civil fines of up to $5 million and the Justice Department could prosecute, with violators facing fines up to $1 million and two years in prison. Money collected in fines would flow into a fund to help low-income families pay energy bills through the LIHEAP program. Price increases genuinely tied to higher wholesale, replacement, or operating costs would have been exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: If enacted, the main beneficiaries would be consumers who buy gasoline and heating fuels during supply emergencies — typically after hurricanes, refinery outages, or wars — who would gain a federal tool against extreme price spikes. Low-income households would indirectly benefit because collected penalties would fund LIHEAP energy assistance. Honest small fuel marketers might also benefit from competitors being barred from extreme emergency markups, and they face a lower penalty cap than large suppliers.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for a supplier to raise the price of crude oil, gasoline, or petroleum distillates by an 'unconscionable amount' in an area covered by a presidential emergency proclamation, with price increases substantially attributable to wholesale or replacement costs, operational costs, or market conditions carved out.

Allows the President to declare an 'abnormal market disruption' — for example from extreme weather, a natural disaster, strike, war, or national emergency — triggering the price-gouging prohibition for specified periods of up to 30 days, renewable.
Directs fines and penalties collected under the Act into a Consumer Relief Trust Fund used to fund the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program, which helps low-income households pay energy bills.

analysis.who_pays: The cost would fall on fuel suppliers — from large oil companies to independent retailers — who could face civil fines of up to $5 million (or $500,000 for small independent marketers) and criminal penalties for unconscionable price increases during declared emergencies, and who would bear the burden of FTC compliance and rulemaking.

drawbacks.text: The prohibition has wide exemptions: price increases substantially attributable to wholesale costs, replacement costs, operational costs, or market conditions are allowed, so in most supply-shock scenarios genuine market-driven increases would not be actionable and the ban would reach relatively little conduct.
The ban only applies during a Presidential proclamation, capped at 30-day renewable periods, so gouging outside a declared emergency would remain legal.

Criminal penalties of up to $1,000,000 and two years' imprisonment for pricing decisions create a risk of over-deterrence or harassment of legitimate price setters, a standard objection to anti-gouging statutes that defenders argue would be mitigated by the justifiable-increase safe harbors.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — protecting drivers and home-heating users from exploitative price spikes during emergencies, with penalties funding heating aid for poor households — is real but narrow: the ban would only be in effect during a presidentially declared disruption, and its broad exemptions for wholesale-cost and market-condition increases would make convictions hard to obtain. The cost falls on suppliers who raise prices excessively during emergencies, which is the point of the bill. As written it is a modest consumer safeguard rather than a broad price control.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred the bill to committees and subcommittees in mid-2007, and no committee ever voted to move it to the floor before the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Vito Fossella (R-NY) introduced the Federal Energy Price Protection Act on May 23, 2007, with three Republican cosponsors.

The same day, the House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Education and Labor Committee; it was then sent to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality and, in July 2007, also referred to a subcommittee of the Education and Labor Committee.
No further action was taken; the bill never received a committee vote, a floor vote, or consideration in the Senate, and died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Petroleum suppliers who might raise prices sharply during emergencies, and the members who chose not to move the bill, are better off; no anti-gouging rules or new LIHEAP funding mechanism took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Petroleum suppliers; no anti-gouging rules took effect

for.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral in May 2007 and never reported it out; the bill sat in subcommittee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all four cosponsors were Republicans, but the bill received no recorded votes, so the partisan shape of its fate cannot be measured from the record.

industries.industry: Oil and petroleum suppliers (producers, wholesalers, and large retailers)
industries.note: The bill would expose large suppliers to civil penalties up to $5 million and criminal penalties during declared emergencies for 'unconscionable' price increases beyond their cost and market justifications. Small independent gasoline marketers face a lower $500,000 cap, recognizing their tighter margins.

industries.industry: Low-income households receiving LIHEAP energy assistance
industries.note: Penalties collected under the bill would be deposited into a Consumer Relief Trust Fund to support the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program, adding a funding stream for heating and cooling aid.

They face the same prohibition as large suppliers but with a lower civil penalty cap ($500,000 versus $5 million), acknowledging their limited resources; they could also gain if large suppliers' emergency price spikes were restrained.
